extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour studies, sociolinguistics, conversation analysis, and developmental psychology
extracted.subtask_description: Examine how laughter and 'unlaughter' function rhetorically in interaction: the dimensions and timing of laughter, placement of laughter particles, conversational norms (e.g., troubles-talk), developmental learning of teasing/ridicule, and the social/ideological implications of ridicule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moerman's four dimensions of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can vary along four dimensions: (1) delayed/prompt; (2) few particles/many particles; (3) soft/loud; and (4) slow/rapid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By varying laughter along these dimensions, speakers convey different meanings (e.g., loud, many-particled laughter can mark a verbal insult as joking rather than literal). Use these dimensions to categorize and interpret the communicative force of a laugh.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate timing of laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients should be able to produce 'laughter in an appropriately timed way', coming not too soon or too late after the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing must be delicately coordinated between speakers so recipients 'upgrade' the teller's laughter; poorly timed laughter can miscommunicate uptake or offence (Sacks).

rubrics_metrics.name: Collective/coordinated laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter performs best when 'done together'—to do laughing right, it should be done together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coordinated group laughter signals shared appreciation; analyses should consider synchronization and mutual upgrading of laughs among participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural-appearing/unfeigned laughter
rubrics_metrics.description: The laughter should appear natural and unfeigned if recipients are to indicate genuine pleasure at the joke.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Delivery requires practice and sound judgement; contrived or obviously forced laughter undermines the communicative effect and can alter pragmatic interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter integrated with speech to signal appreciation
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter can be mixed with words to produce the rhetoric of appreciation (e.g., repeating the punch-line amidst particles of laughter to indicate appreciation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for repetition of punchlines, laughter particles embedded in turn-construction, and post-punchline amplification as markers that recipients are signaling enjoyment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Placement of laughter particles for precise conversational meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The placement of laughter particles can perform subtle conversational functions (e.g., a laugh may precede an obscene word to signal awareness that it might give offence; laughter particles can specifically accompany numbers to indicate surprise).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze exact positioning of particles relative to lexical items—particles are not merely scattered but precisely placed to mark politeness, surprise, mitigation, or to highlight the relevant element of the turn.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as mitigation/softening device
rubrics_metrics.description: A laugh or a smile can mitigate an utterance (such as a complaint or direct request) that otherwise recipients may find too strong or too direct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Laughter particles must be precisely placed within utterances to indicate exactly what is being softened; treat laughter as part of politeness rhetoric (Brown & Levinson) rather than merely a reaction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as argumentative and justificatory device
rubrics_metrics.description: Laughter particles can be used to convey argumentative meaning, sometimes ambiguously and without spelling out all assumptions; laughter can downgrade the importance of complaints and help justify the speaker's stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use examples where laughter frames a complaint/story to analyze how speakers reduce moral culpability or distance themselves from claims (e.g., laughing while recounting prejudiced behaviour to imply amusement rather than outrage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Troubles-talk laughter signals coping, not amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: In problems-talk, interpolated particles of laughter can indicate that speakers with serious illnesses are 'coping' (Jefferson's 'brave laughter'); laughter here is not funny but facilitates serious talk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recipients are not supposed to repeat the speaker's laughter in such contexts; echoing it would belittle the problems. Identify end-position laughs and subsequent recipient responses as evidence of 'humourless' laughter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlaughter as rhetorical presence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlaughter denotes a display of not laughing when laughter might otherwise be expected, conveying significant absence (e.g., silence, cutting in, forbidding expression) and thereby communicating disapproval or serious stance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat silence and facial expression as active communicative moves; examples include cutting the topic to halt enjoyment, or a po-face that simultaneously signals understanding and disapproval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Varieties of unlaughter and gradations of (un)amusement
rubrics_metrics.description: There are many ways of displaying unlaughter: withholding laughter, delayed and meanly particled laughter, groans, deliberately slow 'oh-hah-hah', verbal put-downs ('we are not amused'), and forbidding expressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When coding responses, include subtle forms (meanly particled, groan) as distinct from full silent unlaughter; consider how gradations map onto levels of disapproval.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unlaughter requires congruent nonverbal expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Verbal unlaughter (e.g., saying 'we are not amused') requires an appropriately forbidding facial expression; conflicting signals (a smile plus a verbal claim of non-amusement) will undermine the unlaughter's force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess alignment of verbal and facial/body signals when interpreting unlaughter; mismatches can neutralize intended rhetorical effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule can target unlaughter and reverse its force
rubrics_metrics.description: Unlaughter can itself become the target of ridicule—people may laugh at the unlaughing figure (e.g., mocking Queen Victoria's hauteur), turning disapproval into an object of amusement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Account for meta-rhetorical moves where performers or observers refract unlaughter into comedic material, recruiting audiences into laughing at the non-laugher.

rubrics_metrics.name: Humour's dual social/anti-social function
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour (and laughter) is both social and anti-social: it can bring people together (shared amusement) and divide them (ridicule); the laughter's meaning derives from wider rhetorical context rather than from laughter itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating humour, analyze contextual and ideological framing: identical laughter forms can unify within one context and ostracize in another; avoid purely stimulus-response accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Children learn the rhetoric of laughter through interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Children learn how to laugh appropriately and to understand others' laughter by interacting with and imitating older speakers (e.g., family); laughter must be learnt as part of language/social practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study parent–child interaction for modeling, imitation, and corrective uses of laughter; look for apprenticeship patterns where adults' laughter teaches acceptable targets and timing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parental teasing/mockery as a socialisation/disciplinary technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Parents may use teasing and mockery to discipline children and teach social codes; teasing can make children more independent and is used cross-culturally by caregivers (e.g., Kulali mothers rarely use physical chastisement but tease).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine teasing episodes for regulatory function (making demands, discouraging unwanted requests), and consider cultural variation and pleasurable aspects for caregivers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research framing: developmental stages vs. social apprenticeship
rubrics_metrics.description: Developmental psychologists sometimes describe humour emergence in staged cognitive terms (children reach a stage before 'real' humour), while sociocultural accounts emphasize apprenticeship and social learning of humour.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about theoretical commitments when analyzing children's humour: a stage-based cognitive interpretation differs in implications from an interactional/apprenticeship perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ridicule as a possible necessary social function (Bergson)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ridicule may lie at the heart of humour and serve a necessary social function: helping to maintain social order by disciplining or correcting deviations; without ridicule social behaviour risks rigidity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include consideration of ideological implications: treating ridicule as necessary contrasts with ideological positivist views that see ridicule as detachable and undesirable. Use historical and cross-cultural evidence to assess the claim.
